metadata.title: Monna Pixelisa
metadata.info: A living study in color and permanence through the pulse of Bitcoin. Four eternal interpretations of the Mona Lisa, stored on a single rare Satoshi. Each variant processes the same image by recursing through a distinct monochrome palette—cyan, green, purple, red—while the Bitcoin network dictates their visual pixelation in real time. The Mechanism: Every 60 seconds, the work queries the current block's data: number of transactions and total weight. These metrics determine the pixel size (from 2x2 to 16x16). High network congestion fragments the image into larger pixels; peak activity adds noise through ordered dithering. The Mona Lisa becomes more abstract as Bitcoin becomes more active. The Permanence: Four color studies, one rare satoshi. Each palette reveals different aspects of the source image through color quantization—what survives in cyan fades into red, what shines in green fades into purple. The inscriptions are linked recursively, calling upon the same base image but transforming it through four lenses that will exist as long as Bitcoin exists. The Statement: This is not generative art with artificial randomness. This is deterministic visual archaeology—the blockchain writes the aesthetic, block by block. The collector doesn't own a static image; he owns four perpetual algorithms that translate network activity into visual degradation, four simultaneous meditations on how data shapes perception. On-chain. Recursive. Reactive. Forever.

metadata.Title: Naked
metadata.Description: This digital painting continues the long tradition in art history of the reclining nude, a subject explored from Titian's Venus of Urbino to Manet's Olympia. The figure's relaxed pose and direct gaze echo classical compositions but the bold, gestural brushwork and the palette give it a distinctly contemporary energy. The work bridges the gap between traditional life drawing and modern digital experimentation while the human form remains a vital subject for artists exploring humanity.

metadata.description:
Joe (@JoeOrdinals) is a dopamine junkie and Bitcoin artist renowned for his distinctive scribbles and hand-drawn works, created as an anonymous creator who often draws inspiration under the influence of various natural substances like mushrooms and weed.

He emerged as the leading figure behind the FinePepes collection—a decentralized, organic collaboration of over 500 artists that produced a 10k Ordinals series etched on-chain—and founded the Ordinal Rabbits community to foster discussions and creative events, while blending digital innovation with physical art through exhibitions featuring acrylic canvases, sketchbooks, custom masks, and coins.

An early Ordinals adopter, Joe emphasizes fun, community-driven projects and cultural vibes, establishing himself as a dynamic contributor to Bitcoin-native art and ecosystem growth.

metadata.Title: Mycelioid PRSM
metadata.Description: “Mycelioid PRSM” is the 11th entry in a long-term art journal on the blockchain. Responding dynamically to Bitcoin's ongoing development, each new block triggers a sequence that reshapes the work. || “Mycelioid PRSM” presents a process that continually adjusts its own state, seen through the lens of an analytical instrument. Something organic is placed within a model, its continuity divided into measurable fragments. The image does not depict growth itself, but the condition that emerges when a living process is subjected to observation. || Time here is non-linear and recursive. Each moment carries traces of previous states, as if the system were constantly overwriting its own memory. Organic motion crosses sharp boundaries without acknowledging them, reinforcing the sense that the process persists independently of the structure used to observe it. || The image is divided into six triangular fields that function as an imposed analytical framework rather than a compositional choice. These divisions do not originate from the system itself; they act as an external geometry, a measuring grid placed over a living process. The triangle subtly references simulation and rendering — the moment when continuity is translated into discrete form. || Under sustained observation, the work exposes a secondary mode of behavior.

metadata.This Photo: My Father took this photo of me, one of his favorites, with his Nikon FM2 when I was ~2-3 years old. This was my view growing up. A person's view/environment greatly impacts the way they evolve to see the world. I am extremely grateful that this once upon a time summer lake cabin, was my year round home that gave me the privilege of such a view.
metadata.My Photography History: My father's passion of photography passed onto me and flourished in me. Thus far, throughout my life I mainly used three different types of handheld cameras and five smartphone integrated cameras. I'm not sure which camera my first click was on, my Dad's Nikon or my Mom's Pentax.
metadata.Nikon FM2: I remember how he tried to teach me how to use the manual focus, and how I didn't understand it at first, but once I did, I thought it was neat. More memories of using the Nikon include taking action shots of our dog, Monty, and then developing them in my High School darkroom. We also used a special shutter release cord to take time elapsed photos of the stars.
metadata.Pentax IQ zoom: For 1988 Christmas, my Dad got my Mom a Pentax IQZoom 60 camera. She was elated. The camera was a classic compact automatic with a 38-60mm zoom. I was 3.75 years old at the time, and hadn't known at the time, that I would eventually be allowed to use it, and love it. Taking pictures with a film camera was much more selective and conservative than the digital era of today, with the ability to take so many pictures without much care of wasting film. A photo I fondly remember taking with this camera was at a cousin's wedding in 1991, of my Mom and Dad on the shore of Lake Mendota at sunset, it turned out amazing, and we've had a print displayed of it since then.
metadata.Kodak EasyShare Z730: My first camera I bought on my own in 2005, the same year it came out. A digital 5 Megapixel camera that allowed a lot of different manual setting options. My favorite being the shutter speed because I love taking night photos. I still have this camera.
metadata.Smartphones: Samsung, HTC, LG Nexus, Pixel 4a,6a,8a. I didn't buy my first smartphone until I was living in Russia in 2015.
metadata.History of Photography: A short concise timeline of the evolution of photography.
metadata.1820s-1830s | Foundational Chemical Phot: Joseph Nicéphore Niépce creates the first permanent photograph. He used Bitumen of Judea (naturally occurring tar-like asphalt) that hardens when exposed to light, applied to metal or stone. Louis Deaguerre's 1839 daguerreotype (silver-plated copper sensitized with iodine vapor). Both substances, had very low light sensitivity that used the same process. Hand-prepare plate → long exposure (minutes to hours) → develop chemically (heat or mercury vapor) → fix with salt or hypo. Each image was a unique physical object with extreme detail but no negative.
metadata.1840s-1870s | Negative-postive systems: Calotype (Talbotype) - Invented by WIlliam Henry Fox Talbot; used paper negatives coated with silver iodide. Wet-plate Collodion - Glass plates coated with collodion (a syrupy nitrocellulose solution) mixed with light-sensitive salts. Process - Coat plate or paper with light-sensitive chemistry → expose while still wet → immediately develop and fix → produce multiple prints via contact printing. Field photographers carried portable darkrooms. Wet-plate images had to be exposed and developed before the plate dried. Shorter exposures, sharper details/images, and reproducibility. Photography spreads into science, documentation, and portraiture.
metadata.1870s-1910s | Dry plates, roll film, and: Gelatin emulsion dry glass plates (Richard Leach Maddox, Charles Bennet), faster and more stable. Flexible plastic roll film coated with gelatin silver emulsion (George Eastman/Kodak). Simple fixed-focus cameras → Load film → take many exposures without reloading → send film to lab → standardized emulsions → contact prints. Photography becomes consumer-friendly, snapshot culture emerges.
metadata.1920s-1940s | Miniaturization & Precisio: Oscar Barnack (Leica) Adopted 35mm cine-derived film (1890s, Thomas Edison/William Dickson), precision lenses, rangefinders, faster shutters. Measure or estimate exposure → capture fast, candid images → develop negatives → enlarge onto photographic paper. Supports photojournalism, street photography, and modern visual storytelling.
metadata.1950s-1970s | Color Photography Maturity: Color film → Multi-layer emulsions sensitive to red, green and blue light. Dye couplers → Chemicals that form colored dyes during development. Slide (reversal) film → Produces a positive image directly, i.e. WYSIWYG, e.g. Kodachrome
metadata.1980s-1990s | Digital Transition: Turning light into digital data using a silicon chip. Light hits each pixel creates electrical charge proportional to brightness. Charge-Coupled Device (CCD) - Charges are shifted across the chip to a single output amplifier. Complementary Metal-Oxide Semiconductor (CMOS) - Pixels are read individually, each has its own amplifier and readout circuitry. CCD defined early digital imaging quality; CMOS enabled modern digital and computational photography. Analog-to-digital conversion → translates electrical signals into numeric values → stored on disk → post-processing replaces much of the darkroom → images output to printers or displays.
metadata.2000s-present | Computational Imaging Ec: Driven by exponential improvement in silicon chips. Smartphones, multi-sensor arrays, AI-assisted algorithms. Capture image bursts → computational merging (High Dynamic Range (HDR), stacking, depth simulation) → automated enhancement → immediate global distribution and archiving via networks and cloud platforms.
metadata.35mm film vs. Megapixels: Physical vs. Digital | Black and white 35mm film reached the equivalent quality of 20-25 Megapixels by the late 1930s and by the late 60s for color. It wasn't until 2005-07 that high-end digital, 12 MP, became a practical 35mm quality substitute for most uses, and 2008-10 for 20-24 MP full-frame digital that matched or exceeded 35 mm film in resolution, consistency, and workflow.
metadata.Megapixels (MP): Define how many pixels you have, i.e. How much information you have, e.g. 5000x4000px = 20 MP
metadata.Pixels Per Inch (PPI): Defines how big those pixels print, i.e. How big you spread it
metadata.Dots Per Inch (DPI): Defines how the printer sprays ink, i.e. How the printer paints it
metadata.GIMP (raster editor): Uses DPI when it's actually PPI
metadata.Megapixels needed for quality Posters: Recommended MP and PPI for common poster sizes. Rule of thumb → 300 PPI = magazines / close inspection. 150-200 PPI = posters viewed at arm's length or farther
metadata.18x24 inches: 240 PPI → 10MP . . or . . 180 PPI → 6MP (still looks good on a wall)
metadata.24x36 inches (movie poster): PPI DPI → 17 MP . . or  . . 150 PPI → 10 MP (still looks good on a wall)
metadata.Rule of thumb: 300 PPI → magazines / close inspection and 150–200 PPI → posters viewed at arm’s length or farther
metadata.600x600 px | Digitally: A digital screen displays images pixel-for-pixel, not inch-for-inch. When a 600×600 image is shown on screen, the software maps those 600 pixels to the screen’s pixels. How big it looks physically on screen depends entirely on the screen’s pixel density, not the image. On a 100 PPI monitor, the 600 px will look ~6x6 inches wide.
metadata.Physical Scalability 600x600px 300 PPI: Confined within the already set MP, the larger you make the image, the more blurry it becomes.
metadata.Digital Scalability 600x600px 300 PPI: The image is always 600×600 pixels. The 300 PPI tag is ignored. It can be displayed any physical size depending on screen pixel density (small on high-PPI screens, large on low-PPI screens) without gaining detail.
metadata.Digital panel wall - LED video wall: Controllers scale and map the 600×600 image across many tiles. Low effective PPI (large pixel pitch) lets the image fill many feet. Detail does not increase; pixels are simply larger and meant for distance viewing.
metadata.Artistically: Photographing the wall can work to physically scale a possible enlarged print, but it's not equivalent to native print resolution.

metadata.Collection Created: I originally created the children of this inscription using this photo after returning (2011) to the US from teaching English for two years in Ethiopia. I used GIMP to do the editing.
metadata.Originally: Called the 'Clock Tower' the 'Great Clock' and the 'Great Bell' aka 'Big Ben'
metadata.Following: A fire that destroyed the medieval, 1050, Anglo-Saxon Palace
metadata.Westminster Hall: Built in 1097 survived the fire, still exists today.
metadata.Victorian Rebuild: In Neo-Gothic designed by Charles Barry, A.W.N. Pugin
metadata.Clock Tower: Renamed 'Elizabeth Tower' in 2012 on Queen Elizabeth II Diamond Jubilee (60th anniversary)
metadata.Overtime: The Tower slightly drifted off center
metadata.From 2017-2022: Major restorations were made, stabilizing and refurbishing the Tower and Clock.
metadata.Big Ben: The Great Bell's nickname has two theories.
metadata.First Theory: Chief Commissioner of Works Sir Benjamin Hall when the bell was installed. He was physically big and boisterous.
metadata.MPs: Jokingly referred to him as 'Big Ben'
metadata.He gave: A long booming speech defending the project
metadata.Second Theory: Famous heavyweight boxer of the time Benjamin Caunt, also nicknamed 'Big Ben'
metadata.Big Ben Slang: Was already common for something massive and forceful
metadata.Caunt: Was far more famous to ordinary Londoners than Sir Benjamin Hall.
metadata.Victorians: Frequently named machines after boxers, racehorses, and generals.
metadata.The nickname: For the bell began immediately after installation.
metadata.Artist Story: Following the 2009 spring/summer of my TEFL certification in Barcelona. I took a job in Ethiopia. I was supposed to be able to get a temporary Business Visa upon arrival, which would be able to transition into a long term business visa without leaving the country. But the officials at the Addis Ababa airport decided to give me a temporary Tourist Visa instead. Literally a handwritten difference from a VB to a VT. This caused an inconvenient trip back to D.C. to obtain the correct visa type from the Ethiopian embassy. Getting the Visa went smoothly and I was able to utilize the roundtrip ticket that I had purchased for $300 more than the one way trip. On my return I had a 15 hour layover in London beginning at 6am. I took the Underground to Queensway station. Arriving to a foggy London green space, with very little pedestrian traffic and what I thought were Royal horses out for a trot.  I was carrying my large JanSport backpack packed to the gills, a medium sized CamelBak, shoulder strapped back and front respectively (alternating throughout the walk), and my guitar which I was reunited with when my Dad brought it to DC.  Instead of storing my belongings in one of the many possible locations, I carried them some 12 miles while I walked along the Thames to Tower Bridge and back to Elizabeth Tower in time to get this photo of the Great Clock striking 12, noon. Part of my motivation to get a photo of the clock striking 12 was the symbolism it shares with the Doomsday Clock.
metadata.The Bulletin Of the Atomic Scientists: A nonprofit founded in 1945 (Originally The Bulletin Of the Atomic Scientists of Chicago, 'of Chicago' dropped in 1947) by scientists who worked on the Manhattan Project (nuclear weapons). They believed the public and policymakers needed independent, scientifically grounded warnings about their consequences. The Bulletin's mission is to warn the public and policymakers about existential threats created by humans. The first controlled nuclear chain reaction (12/2/1942) was carried out by the Metallurgical Laboratory (Manhattan Project), in a squash court beneath the west stands at Stagg Field, University of Chicago, under the direction of Enrico Fermi. The Bulletin was originally a mimeographed newsletter not published annually. First, irregularly, as-needed, then became monthly, and finally bimonthly.
metadata.The Doomsday Clock: Created in 1947 by the Bulletin, the closer the Doomsday Clock is to midnight, the closer humanity is to an irreversible collapse of global civilization. It takes into account Nuclear Risk, Climate Change, Emerging Tech Risks (AI, bioengineering), and Geopolitical Instability & Misinformation. It's a warning signal, not a prediction, used to pressure governments and the public toward risk reduction and policy action. The current clock sits at 85 secconds to midnight, the closest it's ever been to symbolic global catastrophe. The clock is set annually.
metadata.Official Bulletin statement: The Doomsday Clock is a design that warns the public about how close we are to destroying our world with dangerous technologies of our own making. It is a metaphor, a reminder of the perils we must address if we are to survive on the planet
metadata.1947 - 7 minutes: Creation of the atomic age; scientists warn of nuclear weapons' implications.
metadata.1949 - 3 minutes: USSR tests its first atomic bomb, ending the U.S. nuclear monopoly.
metadata.1953 - 2 minutes: U.S. and USSR test hydrogen bombs > massive escalation in destructive power.
metadata.1960 - 7 minutes: Temporary easing after Cold War tensions stabilize post-Sputnik era.
metadata.1963 - 12 minutes: Partial Nuclear Test Band Treaty and post-Cuban Missile Crisis de-escalation.
metadata.1968 - 7 minutes: Vietnam War, arms race intensification, doubts about the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty (NPT) effectiveness.
metadata.1972 - 12 minutes: Strategic Arms Limitation Talk (SALT) and Anti-Ballistic Missile Treaty (ABM) curb nuclear arms growth.
metadata.1974 - 9 minutes: India tests a nuclear weapon, signaling wider nuclear proliferation.
metadata.1980 - 7 minutes: Soviet invasion of Afghanistan; collapse of détente.
metadata.1981 - 5 minutes: Escalating U.S.-Soviet rhetoric and arms buildup under Reagan.
metadata.1984 - 3 minutes: Cold War peak tensions, NATO missile deployments, nuclear war fears.
metadata.1988 - 6 minutes: Intermediate-Range Nuclear Forces Treaty (INF) Treaty signed; U.S.-Soviet arms reductions begin.
metadata.1990 - 10 minutes: Fall of eastern Bloc, reduced superpower confrontation.
metadata.1991 - 17 minutes (farthest ever): End of Cold War, Strategic Arms Reduction Treaty (START), Soviet Union collapse.
metadata.1995 - 14 minutes: Lingering nuclear dangers; stalled disarmament progress.
metadata.1998 - 9 minutes: India and Pakistan conduct nuclear tests.
metadata.2002 - 7 minutes: U.S. withdraws from ABM Treaty, post-9/11 instability.
metadata.2007 - 5 minutes: Nuclear risks + climate change formally added to Clock factors.
metadata.2010 - 6 minutes: New START treaty, international climate talks momentum.
metadata.2015 - 3 minutes: Failure to address climate change; nuclear weapons still central to security.
metadata.2017 - 2.5 minutes: U.S.-Russia tensions, nuclear rhetoric, erosion of arms control.
metadata.2018 - 2 minutes: Breakdown of diplomatic norms; climate and nuclear threats intensify.
metadata.2020 - 100 seconds: Nuclear risk + climate crisis + information warfare.
metadata.2023 - 90 seconds: Russia-Ukraine war, nuclear threats, climate failures, emerging tech risks.
metadata.2025 - 89 seconds: Continued war, AI risk acceleration, weak global cooperation.
metadata.2026, Today, January 27 - 85 seconds: The closest it has ever been to midnight. Escalating global tensions and geopolitical aggression. Weakening and expiration of arms control agreements (New START Treaty expiring). Regional conflicts involving nuclear-armed states. Nuclear modernization and arms races. Climate change risk and inadequate action. Disruptive technologies and artificial intelligence. Biological threats and technology misuse. Failure of leadership and global cooperation.
metadata.Minutes to Seconds: We switched to seconds to convey urgency rather than precision
metadata.The Bulletin has stated repeatedly: The Clock is symbolic, It is not a prediction, It is a communication tool, time units are metaphorical, not literal measures of probability or countdown.
metadata.Artist Statement: The variables the Bulletin currently takes into account are good, but they could add more, given the gigantic special interest industrial complex institutions that have evolved with our civilization and have become ingrained in it. Global Institutions/Elites/Tribes that share no allegiances to nation states other than using them to fulfill their agendas and continued mutual grip on power.
metadata.Military Industrial Complex (MIC): A classical concept referring to the interlinked interests of military institutions (governments, intel. agencies) and defense contractors - Perpetual war, geopolitical influence, and profit-driven conflict.
metadata.Financial Industrial Complex (FIC): Large institutional asset managers, banks, and finance entities that control capital flows, influence policy, and drive economic outcomes like debt slavery and reconstruction profits after wars.
metadata.Tech Industrial Complex (TIC): The network of tech firms, AI platforms, and digital infrastructure that enables surveillance, control systems, programmable money (CBDCs), and profit from digital ecosystems.
metadata.Overarching Network: The Meta-Complex that integrates MIC, FIC and TIC. Within this framework, the industrial complexes are nodes within the Network that perpetuate debt, control, and geopolitical strategy. The meta-complex is the overlay that; aligns incentives across all of them; routes money, power, and policy between them; ensures they reinforce each other rather than operate independently.
metadata.Meta-Complex: The system-of-systems that coordinates and monetizes multiple industrial complexes into a single self-reinforcing power and control loop. No single entity "runs" the meta-complex; it is governed by aligned incentives among transnational elites and institutions, not by a formal command structure. It is run indirectly by interlocking networks of state actors, financial institutions, defense contractors, and technology platforms whose incentives align around power, 0control, and capital preservation.
metadata.Military: Creates instability and justification (conflict, fear, security needs)
metadata.Finance: Monetizes that instability (debt, reconstruction, bailouts, asset capture)
metadata.Technology: Scales and enforces it (surveillance, platforms, compliance systems, 'manufacturing consent')
metadata.Outputs: Of each become the inputs of the others
metadata.Money grows, but more importantly: Control becomes entrenched, risk is socialized, upside is privatized, the loop becomes self-sustaining
metadata.It's not money, money, money: It's power > leverage > durability - with money as the measurable byproduct
metadata.Artist Furthermore: The Bulletin should come up with a more scientific approach that account for these variables. It isn't in the best interests of these variables to come close to a catastrophic event(s) that would collapse the very civilization that slaves to maintain their cushy powerful lifestyles. However the appearance of catastrophe and war can help them attain the Global Order they desire. For being 85 seconds to midnight, global civilization seems pretty good despite the nuances of global powers trying to fulfill their agendas and the micro pockets of relative chaos (war, malnutrition, famine, homelessness). Time is relative and literal an irreversible collapse of global civilization seems at least a half-hour away from midnight. Granted a catastrophic event could quickly take the clock much closer to Doomsday. And although we may have surpassed the point-of-no-return for eventual dramatic human induced climate change, that change will come relatively slow over a period of time, which should allow us to continually adapt to our environments. As is, I believe the Doomsday Clock, makes it appear that our civilization is living on the edge of catastrophe, when in actuality it is much further away, granted one Black Swan event can have a domino effect and take us to the edge rapidly, let's pray that doesn't happen, and if it does, give us the strength to persevere through it.
metadata.Or: This could all just be bullshit, and everything is a crapshoot or a combination thereof.

metadata.Artist Story: Following the 2009 spring/summer of my TEFL certification in Barcelona. I took a job in Ethiopia. I was supposed to be able to get a temporary Business Visa upon arrival, which would be able to transition into a long term business visa without leaving the country. But the officials at the Addis Ababa airport decided to give me a temporary Tourist Visa instead. Literally a handwritten difference from a VB to a VT. This caused an inconvenient trip back to D.C. to obtain the correct visa type from the Ethiopian embassy. Getting the Visa went smoothly and I was able to utilize the roundtrip ticket that I had purchased for $300 more than the one way trip. On my return I had a 15 hour layover in London beginning at 6am. I took the Underground to Queensway station. Arriving to a foggy London green space, with very little pedestrian traffic and what I thought were Royal horses out for a trot.  I was carrying my large JanSport backpack packed to the gills, a medium sized CamelBak, shoulder strapped back and front respectively (alternating throughout the walk), and my guitar which I was reunited with when my Dad brought it to DC.  Instead of storing my belongings in one of the many possible locations, I carried them some 12 miles while I walked along the Thames to Tower Bridge and back to Elizabeth Tower in time to get this photo of the Great Clock striking 12, noon. Part of my motivation to get a photo of the clock striking 12 was the symbolism it shares with the Doomsday Clock.
metadata.The Bulletin Of the Atomic Scientists: A nonprofit founded in 1945 (Originally The Bulletin Of the Atomic Scientists of Chicago, 'of Chicago' dropped in 1947) by scientists who worked on the Manhattan Project (nuclear weapons). They believed the public and policymakers needed independent, scientifically grounded warnings about their consequences. The Bulletin's mission is to warn the public and policymakers about existential threats created by humans. The first controlled nuclear chain reaction (12/2/1942) was carried out by the Metallurgical Laboratory (Manhattan Project), in a squash court beneath the west stands at Stagg Field, University of Chicago, under the direction of Enrico Fermi. The Bulletin was originally a mimeographed newsletter not published annually. First, irregularly, as-needed, then became monthly, and finally bimonthly.
metadata.The Doomsday Clock: Created in 1947 by the Bulletin, the closer the Doomsday Clock is to midnight, the closer humanity is to an irreversible collapse of global civilization. It takes into account Nuclear Risk, Climate Change, Emerging Tech Risks (AI, bioengineering), and Geopolitical Instability & Misinformation. It's a warning signal, not a prediction, used to pressure governments and the public toward risk reduction and policy action. The current clock sits at 85 secconds to midnight, the closest it's ever been to symbolic global catastrophe. The clock is set annually.
metadata.Official Bulletin statement: The Doomsday Clock is a design that warns the public about how close we are to destroying our world with dangerous technologies of our own making. It is a metaphor, a reminder of the perils we must address if we are to survive on the planet

metadata.1990 - 10 minutes: Fall of eastern Bloc, reduced superpower confrontation.

metadata.2015 - 3 minutes: Failure to address climate change; nuclear weapons still central to security.

metadata.2018 - 2 minutes: Breakdown of diplomatic norms; climate and nuclear threats intensify.

metadata.2025 - 89 seconds: Continued war, AI risk acceleration, weak global cooperation.
metadata.2026, Today, January 27 - 85 seconds: The closest it has ever been to midnight. Escalating global tensions and geopolitical aggression. metadata.Artist Statement: The variables the Bulletin currently takes into account are good, but they could add more, given the gigantic special interest industrial complex institutions that have evolved with our civilization and have become ingrained in it. Global Institutions/Elites/Tribes that share no allegiances to nation states other than using them to fulfill their agendas and continued mutual grip on power.
metadata.Military Industrial Complex (MIC): A classical concept referring to the interlinked interests of military institutions (governments, intel. agencies) and defense contractors - Perpetual war, geopolitical influence, and profit-driven conflict.
metadata.Financial Industrial Complex (FIC): Large institutional asset managers, banks, and finance entities that control capital flows, influence policy, and drive economic outcomes like debt slavery and reconstruction profits after wars.
metadata.Tech Industrial Complex (TIC): The network of tech firms, AI platforms, and digital infrastructure that enables surveillance, control systems, programmable money (CBDCs), and profit from digital ecosystems.
metadata.Overarching Network: The Meta-Complex that integrates MIC, FIC and TIC. Within this framework, the industrial complexes are nodes within the Network that perpetuate debt, control, and geopolitical strategy. The meta-complex is the overlay that; aligns incentives across all of them; routes money, power, and policy between them; ensures they reinforce each other rather than operate independently.
metadata.Meta-Complex: The system-of-systems that coordinates and monetizes multiple industrial complexes into a single self-reinforcing power and control loop. No single entity "runs" the meta-complex; it is governed by aligned incentives among transnational elites and institutions, not by a formal command structure. It is run indirectly by interlocking networks of state actors, financial institutions, defense contractors, and technology platforms whose incentives align around power, 0control, and capital preservation.

metadata.body:
Preserving Bitcoin: **A Manifesto**

Nations authored the past. Nations minted our currency.

Bitcoin changed that.

Now money and its history belong to the people.

Transactions are the atomic unit of Bitcoin culture. 

Each one a proof of our freedom, recorded forever.

Satoshi Relics turns transactions into cultural artifacts and puts them in the hands of the many.

Why care about history?

Because a network that cannot author its own story can be rewritten.

We must own our history, or our history will be rewritten for us.

Ordinals make the record ownable.

Ownership makes preservation real.

Satoshi Relics is the Bitcoin preservation collection. 

It ensures our history cannot be confiscated.

Secured by Bitcoin, celebrated by Bitcoin, preserved by Bitcoin.

Preservation is our defiance. Digital artifacts are our shield. Ownership our statement of intent.

This is why Bitcoin exists: a stand against centralized authority. 

Against revisionism. Against censorship.

Bitcoin’s first act set the tone:

"The Times 03/Jan/2009 Chancellor on brink of second bailout for banks"

Satoshi Relics is our assurance that the story stays with the people.

Here, history becomes yours to write.

- Proof of Beauty Studio

metadata.title: Block 99 Coinbase Transaction
metadata.description: The coinbase reward created in Bitcoin’s 99th block. Issued under the same consensus and maturity rules as early post-genesis blocks, this transaction represents the continuation of Bitcoin’s monetary issuance as the network approached full coinbase spendability at block 100. It reflects a system in motion: proof-of-work securing newly minted value on the verge of becoming economically usable.
metadata.author: bc1pun9zz678qjlpujnz4zp8e0rk4pt5myp96gfrwaxqfenz8ta3ukpsh7qqss

metadata.title: Block 50 Coinbase Transaction
metadata.description: The coinbase reward created in Bitcoin’s 50th block. Unlike the genesis coinbase, which is permanently unspendable, this reward followed Bitcoin’s standard issuance rules and became spendable after the network’s coinbase maturity period. It reflects early, working monetary issuance: newly minted value secured by proof-of-work and made transferable by consensus rules.

metadata.Title: clump by OK feat.tsitraton
metadata.Description: tsitraton draws lines before they have meaning. I too sometimes draw patterns before they have meaning, or patterns that have lost their meaning. This painting has no meaning, but there is white space where anyone who wants meaning can freely attach it. These lines are rhythm. A rhythm that has developed over time for tsitraton and okayaman. Some people find it pleasant, others find it unpleasant. That's fine. That's what's good. This is my personal interpretation, but these two line artists stopped the lines just before meaning began to emerge. This resulting work is meaningless, but I named it "clump". It is both plant-like and conceptual. That's what I thought. --- At first, this work was contained within tsitraton's lines. Something was missing. When I went beyond the boundaries, this was the result. Traces of growth over time.

metadata.title: Block 220 Coinbase Transaction
metadata.description: The coinbase reward created in Bitcoin’s 220th block, mined during the network’s first days of operation. Issued under Bitcoin’s original consensus rules, this transaction reflects routine monetary issuance at a time when block production, rewards, and participation were still being discovered in real time. Seen today, it reads as a hidden time capsule, an ordinary block unremarkable in its moment, now preserved as an early trace of Bitcoin learning how to exist in public. Its simple mechanics endure as an unintended historical marker, a quiet artifact from before Bitcoin knew it would be remembered.

Beginning during the early rise of AI generated art, the project pushed back against low effort production by emphasizing process, intent, and deliberate constraint. What began as an art practice has grown into a sustained case study at the intersection of culture and technology. HYAIPE is not finished. It is designed to keep evolving.

Ordinal Dreamers is a long-term conceptual project inscribed on Bitcoin as the first Ordinals release under the HYAIPE umbrella. The works are full-bodied character images, originally generated at high resolution, then deliberately compressed before inscription to adapt to the technical constraints of placing data directly on the Bitcoin blockchain. This process transformed detailed AI outputs into simplified, pixelated artifacts, emphasizing permanence over polish and turning each piece into a symbolic on-chain record rather than a conventional digital illustration. The project is conceptually tied to the future of $ORDI, the first token on Bitcoin Ordinals that helped drive wider adoption of the protocol, and was released as a dormant prophecy. In this way, Ordinal Dreamers functions as both artwork and cultural time capsule, embedding belief, speculation, and patience into characters designed to awaken only when the conditions that inspired them have fully matured.

Dreamers is a portrait-based project within the Bitcoin ordinals ecosystem that studies identity, compression, and cultural meaning under conditions of technical constraint. The series uses a deliberate visual language built from dithering, tone reduction, pixelation, and layered compression, transforming full-scale characters into reduced, memory-like portraits that retain presence while resisting full reconstruction. Paired with a experimental launch framework, the project functions as both an identity study and a live systems experiment at the intersection of art, infrastructure, and Bitcoin-native culture.

Dreamers (Phase 1) is a continuation of the Ordinal Dreamers lineage, introduced as an limited series of 33/333 portraits. The phase marks the genesis of an experimental release framework and focuses on identity in its earliest stage of transformation. Visually, the portraits are set against a solid black background, isolating each character while preserving much of their original color and form. Distortion is minimal, allowing the figures to remain semi-visible as the visual language of compression and reduction begins to emerge.

metadata.About: Dreamers (Phase 2) is a portrait-based continuation of the Ordinal Dreamers lineage, expanding the series into a dual-sided identity system. One side uses clean orange-and-white tones tied to Bitcoin’s base-layer identity, while the other uses black-and-white compression and distortion to represent the token-driven layer surrounding it. The portraits are shaped through processes like dithering, tone reduction, and pixelation, creating images that feel partially remembered rather than fully rendered.

metadata.About: Dreamers (Phase 2) — Side A presents the same set of 111 Dreamers, reintroduced through a stripped-down visual language rooted in the Bitcoin aesthetic. Each piece features the characters on a white background with an orange palette that follows the core visual identity of Bitcoin, emphasizing clarity, signal, and simplicity. These works exist as a direct result of the minting method chosen, where minimal image manipulation was used and dithering served as the primary medium. Instead of heavy distortion or abstraction, Side A preserves the essence of the original Dreamers, translating them into a cleaner, Bitcoin-aligned form that reflects the technical constraints and cultural tone of the chain itself.

Dreamers (Phase 2) — Side B presents the same set of 111 Dreamers through a monochrome black and white palette, aligned with the HYAIPE visual language. While still rooted in the dithered method used across the series, Side B introduces heavier image manipulation, layering distortion and compression to push the characters further into abstraction. The result is a darker, more fragmented version of the Dreamers, shaped directly by the minting method chosen. Conceptually, this side reflects the “black hole” theory of digital assets on Bitcoin, where value and attention are pulled inward and absorbed by the chain. In this state, the Dreamers are no longer just signals of faith, but artifacts caught in the gravitational pull of the token layer, compressed and transformed by the same forces that define the ecosystem around them.

metadata.Terrorism, National Security, News Cycle: One day we're told...Osama bin Laden is enemy number one ...He escapes...a news cycle later it's on to a new enemy, a new crisis. - This quote gained attention post 9/11 for its eerily prescient mention of bin Laden, almost 20 months before the attacks. - Trump later used this to falsely claim the book proved he predicted 9/11 and called for bin Laden's death.
metadata.Health Care: We must have universal healthcare. Just imagine the improved quality of life for our society - Trump endorsed and advocated for universal healthcare, closer to a single-payer system. A stark contrast to his current positions.
metadata.Wealth Tax: I would impose a one-time 14.25% tax on individuals and trusts...over $10 million. It would raise $5.7 trillion and wipe out the national debt. - He claims today it's an outdated idea, and is cutting taxes instead of raising them.
metadata.Gun Control: I generally oppose gun control, but I support the ban on assault weapons and I support a slightly longer waiting period to purchase a gun. - By 2016 Trump flipped to a pro-NRA stance, no gun control measures enacted
metadata.Campaign Finance and Corruption: Our system is broken. Politicians are controlled by their donors. I know it firsthand because I used to be one of the biggest donors. - Precursor to Trump's anti-establishment stance.
metadata.Foreign Policy and Trade: We have to be tough, smart, and fair. If a country is screwing us, we screw them back, hard. - Foreshadowing tariffs.
metadata.Political Parties: The Republicans don't win anymore. The Democrats are a mess. The Reform Party gives people a real chance to have a voice. Both parties are "bought and paid for." Captures his outsider identity and disdain for both major parties - a theme he returned to in 2016. Trump treats America’s two dominant parties less as opposing philosophies and more as two rival franchises feeding at the same money trough—something he says can only be fixed through sweeping campaign-finance surgery, tougher ethics rules, and (if necessary) the rise of a viable third party to keep them honest.
metadata.Missile defense: It's not that a missile defense can be built, it's whether it's the right defense for our times, and I believe the answer is no. He believes smaller hard to trace weapons are the real danger. - However Trump and Congress have just approved the first funding phase of $25B for the new 'Golden Dome' missile defense funding. Which is estimated to cost $175B just to build, and likely $500B to $1T for its full life-cycle cost.

metadata.Title: Latch
metadata.Author's Note: Latch is from Caballero's Book Sculptures, an eight-part series that interrogates the economic, archival and technological structures through which language acquires value. Language is among humanity’s earliest storage technologies — a tool designed to outlast the limits of the body. The book stabilized this function, while digital media transformed language into endlessly reproducible data. Meanwhile, video restored the presence of the speaking voice, long suppressed by print. As cultural memory increasingly migrates toward immaterial networks, the question of how language endures becomes newly urgent. Caballero’s series addresses this question and positions poetry within an evolving continuum of record-keeping systems that extends from the codex to the moving image to cryptographic inscription.This series proposes the book as a sculptural object and will see Caballero print eight different books, each as an edition of one, with a unique ISBN and the anatomy and structure of a traditional book.  The books in this series contain only one poem, printed 197 times in their pages. When taken as integers, the digits in 197 add up eventually to 8, a number that represents abundance.  The works in this series are stunning objects yet remain very authentically books, with a table of contents, an author page and a dedication, which is hand-signed and dedicated to its collector.  The physical books are accompanied by a video work of a single page endlessly turning while Caballero reads the poem (minted onto the Ethereum blockchain via the artist’s own smart contract), in addition to this inscription of the poem onto the Bitcoin blockchain – repositioning poetry within contemporary systems of display, transaction and record. The series documents how our file storage mechanisms have evolved: from page, to pixel, to decentralized ledger.

metadata.title: The First Mining Pool
metadata.description:
The first Bitcoin mining pool was Slush Pool (originally called Bitcoin Pooled Mining Server or Bitcoin.cz Mining), launched by Czech developer Marek Palatinus (known as "Slush") on November 27, 2010. It became publicly operational, and mined its first block on December 16, 2010 — block 97,834. 
-This is widely recognized as the world's first mining pool (confirmed in Bitcoin Wiki, Wikipedia, Braiins Pool's own history, and community retrospectives marking its 15th anniversary in 2025).
Slush Pool is still active today (as Braiins Pool) and has mined over 1.3 million BTC historically.
This Relic tells the story of Block 97,834

metadata.title: Dynamic Hash Mutants
metadata.description: A Living Collection on the Bitcoin Blockchain - Defined by their journey, not by their origin. To stand out in the saturated Bitcoin Ordinals market, we didn't just drop another collection of static images. The Hash-Mutants are exactly 100 extremely lightweight, recursive inscriptions. The artwork is never finished. Every time an Ordinal is bought, sold, or transferred, the Bitcoin network generates a new Transaction ID (TXID). Our on-chain engine reads this TXID in real-time and uses it as a deterministic genetic seed. The artwork literally mutates every time it changes hands.

metadata.Description: 'Immutable Bloom' reflects on women’s strength as a force that cannot be erased.  The veiled figure moves through violets - symbols of resilience and quiet persistence. Her identity is partially concealed, yet her presence is undeniable. Strength here is not loud; it is continuous.  The shimmering surface echoes digital texture and blockchain permanence. In crypto, existence is inscription. Once recorded, it remains.  Like a bloom that returns each season, women’s presence in decentralized spaces is not a trend - it is a structure.  Soft, persistent, immutable.

Official parent inscription and primary on-chain archive of my digital artworks on Bitcoin. This root defines provenance and authenticity for the collection. Grounded in symbolism, intuition, and layered realities.

metadata.Title:: Love Takes Root in the Broken Places
metadata.Description:: She did not grow whole. She grew through - gold tracing every fracture, teal veins carrying what the cracks could no longer contain. The violet blooms didn't wait for repair. They colonized the damage, chose the broken terrain as the only soil worth growing in. Her hearts are not given away. They are cultivated. Transparent, fragile, rooted - each one a visible proof that something living chose her specifically because of where she split open. This is what women's love looks like from the inside: not performance, not sacrifice - but persistent, irrational, breathtaking growth in impossible conditions. She is the garden and the ruin simultaneously. The violets don't mind.

Being delicate isn't her weakness... it’s her armor. In a broken world, her grace is the loudest form of courage. She doesn't just survive the shadows; she makes them bloom.

Embodying anguish and longsuffering, perhaps she is asking for just one more day of strength to carry on. There’s duality of color in her hair and eyes, in alternating gold and violet - a nod to the perception of women's multiple roles in society.

In this collage, I wanted to strip back the layers of female identity shaped by pop culture. The surface is filled with symbols of the exhausting pressure we face: the naive ideal of a plastic unicorn, the impossible Superwoman standard, and exposed flesh that highlights the physical pain of chasing perfection. metadata.Title: Vida de Victoria
metadata.Medium: Digital collage animation (GIF), created in Procreate Part of the Visible Violets Collection
metadata.Description: This digital collage animation honors the life and legacy of my paternal grandmother, Pilar Mora, the youngest of four daughters who rose from modest beginnings to become an educator, psychologist, and later a judge presiding over cases involving minors in juvenile detention centers in Mexico. Her professional life reflects a sustained commitment to youth advocacy, education, and social reform.  She married Rubén Mora, also from a humble background. Throughout their 65 year marriage, they supported one another’s intellectual and civic pursuits. With her partnership, he pursued legal studies and became one of the founding members of the first lawyers’ association in the State of Mexico. Together, their lives reflect a shared trajectory of upward mobility through education and public service.  Central to this work is the metaphor of cultivation. My grandmother maintained an expansive home garden, portions of which are incorporated into this composition. The flowers function as symbolic extensions of her life’s work, embodying nurture, continuity, femininity, and generational growth. In addition to cultivating land, she raised six children, six grandchildren, and eight great grandchildren, forming a living lineage that continues to expand.  Included in the composition is Lola, her youngest daughter, who was born with a cognitive health condition and has remained under my grandmother’s lifelong care. Now approaching fifty years of age, well beyond her initial life expectancy, Lola’s life reflects my grandmother’s sustained devotion. In her efforts to secure proper care and education for her daughter, my grandmother contributed to the founding of one of the first schools for children with special needs in Toluca, Mexico, extending her advocacy beyond her own family.  The butterflies present in the animation reference both transformation and inheritance. They also acknowledge my great grandfather, Luis Camarena González, an entomologist and artist who conducted butterfly collection expeditions and incorporated specimens into his work. His influence introduced my grandmother to both scientific inquiry and aesthetic preservation, themes that reverberate through this piece.  The source materials include archival family photographs: an image from my grandparents’ wedding day, Lola holding a flower picked from the family ranch, multiple flowers grown in my grandmother’s home garden, a flower photographed in Maui representing geographic reach and continuity, and butterflies collected and preserved by her father. These materials were digitally manipulated and assembled into an animated GIF using Procreate, extending my grandmother’s decades long practice of handmade photo collages into a contemporary digital format.  This work situates personal lineage within broader themes of female agency, intergenerational resilience, disability advocacy, and the act of cultivation, both literal and metaphorical. Through archival material and digital intervention, Vida de Victoria serves as both tribute and record of the victorious life of Maria del Pilar Victoria.

We Persist explores the female body as a territory of resistance, memory, and transformation. Through the symbolism of doors and thresholds, I reflect on the social, emotional, and structural barriers women continue to face. I am drawn to the frustration of closed spaces and the strength it takes to push them open. Through my work, I honor the women who insisted and opened doors before us, and I believe in keeping those doors open for us and for those who come next.

metadata.Description: “I Am Not Your Surface”, a self-portrait artwork embodies the quiet rebellion of the feminine body against expectation, visibility, and possession. The absence of identity is intentional, she refuses to be read, categorized, or consumed. Here, femininity is neither object nor ornament but a force that mutates, resists, and reclaims space.  She exists beyond surface. She exists beyond permission. She exists on her own terms.

metadata.Title: She Remains In Violet
metadata.Description: This work is a meditation on “presence” — on the quiet endurance of women whose bodies have been regulated, whose voices have been silenced, and whose existence has been politicized. Immersed in violet, the figure stands between memory and resistance. Violet here is not merely a color; it is a state of being — a bruise, a twilight, a threshold between disappearance and permanence. As an Iranian woman, I carry within me the memory of silenced voices and unfinished lives. This piece speaks to a lived experience in which a woman’s very existence has long been contested, and yet she continues to remain. She does not shout. She remains. And in remaining, she resists.

metadata.title: Soul Dance by EP
metadata.description_1: Soul Dance is a fully on-chain generative artwork on Bitcoin. It's not an image. It's not a video. It's a program that lives forever on the blockchain—and it plays music. Every new Bitcoin block mined changes everything. Harmonic scale, key, rhythm, bass pattern, drum pattern. The block height becomes the composer. Bitcoin chooses the music. That music is then translated into visual pixels by a CPPN neural network. The musical phase enters the network as input. The network returns colors and pixels. What you see on the screen is the sound, translated into visual art.
metadata.description_2: When the kick drum hits, a radial wave expands from the center of the canvas. As the buildup grows, the canvas distorts. When the drop comes—silence for a beat, then explosion. Audio and visuals are not in sync. They are the same thing. Each track is a complete structure: Intro → Main → Breakdown → Buildup → Drop → Outro. 88 bars. A DJ set generated from scratch with each block. No servers. No cloud. No external dependencies. The audio code (Tone.js) and the visual code (p5.js) are also inscribed on Bitcoin as recursive inscriptions. The only thing it reads from the outside: the current block number. You own the satoshi on which the work is engraved. As long as Bitcoin exists, Soul Dance will play. No maintenance. No subscriptions. No one can turn it off. This is what fully on-chain art means.

metadata.Description: Underpainting is part of Chapter Two of Non Finito, made alongside Underdrawing. The title nods to traditional painting preparatory stages, the imperceptible layers that hold everything together. Underpainting treats code as a textural tool, forming a portrait that is deliberately kept in an incomplete state, through smears, strokes, and digital artifacts. Viewers can move through layers, animate outputs, reroll versions, and keep the work alive. From non finito to infinito.
metadata.Technical: High-resolution underlayer plus generative layers built in vanilla Canvas2D, with no external libraries. The underlayer is split into five binary chunks, fetched in parallel and stitched back together through recursion. All files live on a single uncommon sat, with binaries inscribed under the Studio parent and the artwork under the Non Finito parent. The background texture reads live block data via /r/blockheight and /r/blockinfo: block hash seeds fibre and grain placement and changes every block, while transaction count sets fibre density. All other layers use open randomness within defined ranges. The code overlay is self-referencing: the artwork displays its own running source as a visual layer. High-resolution PNG export is available at native scale. The animation, which can be played at any resolution, consists of a phased cycle (watery, solid, reveal) driven by paint physics, where drips sample from underlying colours and are subject to gravity. Format is 9:16, consistent across the Non Finito series.

metadata.Description: Underdrawing is part of Chapter Two in the Non Finito series, alongside Underpainting. The title refers to traditional painting's preparatory drawings, usually hidden beneath the finished work. Underdrawing treats Bitcoin as canvas, and code as a sketching tool: construction lines and feature marks build a portrait, while first touches of paint define its outline by contrast. The work is deliberately unfinished. Viewers can move through layers, watch the timelapse for each output, reroll versions, and keep the piece alive. From non finito to infinito.
metadata.Technical: Single HTML file on an uncommon sat, with no external assets beyond p5.js v1.9.2, loaded recursively from /content/7e37766541506810ba6399c4b2735121f508bd9209df43dd200bf2316b014594i0. The paper texture reads live block data via /r/blockheight and /r/blockinfo: block hash seeds fibre and grain placement and changes every block, while transaction count sets fibre density. All other layers use open randomness within defined ranges, producing an infinite number of unique outputs. The silhouette is built from a hand-traced outline stored as coordinates in the code and altered in position and shape with every reroll. The code overlay is self-referencing: the artwork displays its own running source as a visual layer. Timelapse is a post-render replay built with reveal masks over the finished frame. Resolution is kept in sync across output scales (1x to 4x), with high-resolution PNG export at native scale. Format is 9:16, consistent across the Non Finito series.

metadata.Title: OOPARTS #29 quiet moment
metadata.Description: photo / Nikon D750 / - Compressing the quiet everyday. Lowering the resolution of reality allows the unreality to seep in. - / This work intentionally degrades the most basic "device for the act of seeing"—a window—found in the quiet of everyday life, through excessive compression. As a result, the landscape is reduced to unrealistic particles, and the "continuity" and "transparency" that reality should have possessed peel away. What remains is something raw, yet with low resolution. I thought that this might be the true nature of what we truly "see."  The same goes for memories. Perhaps it's a virtual reality world tailored to our own convenience.

metadata.Special Sat: Inscribed on a Pizza Alpha Sat. There are only 10K Pizza Alpha sats out of the 1 Trillion Pizza Sats in existence from the first real world transaction using Bitcoin to purchase two large pizzas from Papa John's for 10K Btc on May 22, 2010.

metadata.Inspiration to make this: Oil plays a huge role in our civilization. I wanted to know how much we've used, and how much we have left.
metadata.Art Disclosure: Used GhatGPT to help make the image concepts, skeleton, skull, oil barrels, gas nozzles, and fire. Then I sized, traced/painted the images as I wanted on Procreate. Added text on GIMP.
Main Sources: Private Industry Datasets (Rystad, Wood Mackenzie, S and P Global Commodity Insights)
metadata.Oil: Ironically, we have about as much proven oil reserves left as we have consumed.
metadata.What we have used: We produced/consumed 1.76 trillion barrels of oil (bbl) from 1859 to 2025.
metadata.What we have left: We have about 1.72 trillion bbl of proven reserves left.
24% - 11.1 yrs - Light and Sweet - 410 billion bbl
20% - 9.2 yrs. - Light and Sour - 340 billion bbl
14% - 6.5 yrs. - Medium and Sweet - 240 billion bbl
16% - 7.4 yrs. - Medium|Heavy and Sour - 270 billion bbl
Finding new reserves?: Yes, around 8-12 billion bbl per year
Most additions come from existing fields or harder resources
Most new discoveries are harder to obtain
Harder to obtain, usually harder to refine, overall its more expensive
Years of Oil left (Based on a 0.8% annua: 44 years is roughly the upper-bound for currently proved reserves.
If discoveries stay below consumption, the true countdown will drift down slowly at first, then faster and faster.

metadata.Title: Petro Thinker
metadata.Special Sat: Inscribed on a Pizza Omega Sat. There are only 10K Pizza Omega Sats out of the 1 Trillion Pizza Sats in existence from the first real world transaction using Bitcoin to purchase two large pizzas from Papa John's for 10K Btc on May 22, 2010.
metadata.What is an Omega Sat?: Each Bitcoin has 100 million Sats in it. An Omega Sat is the LAST Sat in each Bitcoin.
metadata.Inspiration to make this: The Thinker - Contemplating how we undervalued finite oil, and our excessive use of it, which catalyzed a change in our ecosystem putting us on a course of an alternate world that wouldn't have existed otherwise.
metadata.Art Disclosure: I used Craiyon.com to help create the gas pump/nozzle and earth imagery, and I traced/painted a skeleton/skull made by it.
metadata.Historically: We have priced oil cheaply, without viable substitutes for all the ‘work’ it enables us to do. Cheap oil is so ingrained that we are forced to keep it cheap, because we didn’t develop society around expensive oil, we developed it on cheap oil, and now we can’t afford to truly value it.
metadata.ChatGPT: Put my thesis into Academic, Punchy and Provocative statements.
metadata.Academic / Neutral: Modern industrial growth has been strongly conditioned by the availability of relatively cheap liquid fuels. Petroleum is a finite, depleting stock, yet it remains difficult to substitute in several high-power, mobile, and time-critical domains — construction equipment, mining, freight logistics, and key petrochemical feedstocks. As a result, economic systems, infrastructure, and settlement patterns have been optimized around low oil prices and reliable access, often without a persistent 'scarcity premium' showing up in long-run, inflation-adjusted retail prices. This creates path dependence > as oil-intensive capital and supply chains accumulate, the short-run costs of repricing oil upward—or of supply disruption—become increasingly disruptive. Societies therefore tend to treat oil as a normal commodity rather than as a strategically enabling, finite input, not because its role is minor, but because affordability and continuity constraints are now embedded in the structure of the economy.
metadata.Punchy: We built modern civilization on cheap oil—a finite resource. Not because oil isn’t insanely valuable, but because we never built full substitutes for the work it does > diesel machinery, mining, freight, and the chemical backbone of materials. Cheap oil is now baked into our roads, suburbs, supply chains, and equipment fleets. And even though oil is finite, its price has often behaved like it isn’t—more shock-driven than steadily scarcity-driven—so we keep treating it like an ordinary commodity. If we priced it like a truly finite, strategic input, the whole system would feel the shock.
metadata.Provocative: Oil is the quiet foundation under almost everything physical—and we price a finite, one-time endowment like it’s just another consumable. We did it for so long that “cheap oil” became a law of nature > cities sprawled, supply chains stretched, and industry standardized around a fuel we still can’t fully replace for heavy work. The inflation-adjusted price doesn’t steadily scream “running out”; it mostly spikes during crises—so the illusion of abundance persists. Now we’re trapped, we have to keep it cheap, because we built a society that can’t afford to treat a finite keystone input as finite.
metadata.Alternate History: Imagine we’d treated oil from the beginning as a finite, premium 'work fuel' instead of a cheap default. Cities would have grown tighter and more local by design, because distance would have always had a real cost. Freight and industry would still exist at scale, but optimized earlier around efficiency > rail and electrified corridors where possible, and liquid fuels reserved for the jobs that truly needed them. Construction sites would look familiar, but the machines would have evolved faster to do more work per gallon, and alternatives would have matured sooner because the economics never let waste feel normal. In that world, today’s transition wouldn’t feel like an emergency or a shock—it would feel like the continuation of a long-standing assumption > oil is powerful, finite, and used deliberately.
metadata.Blood for Oil: If we had gone down the 'Alternate History' path, would we have more or less 'war for oil'?
metadata.Innovations: Expensive oil would have brought competition to innovate better and better alternatives faster, leading to cheaper and cheaper oil, maybe even nullifying our dependency and need we have for it. But that wouldn't be good for the oil business.
Disclaimer: I have nothing against Oil except for our disregard to value it properly, our excessive addiction to it and its excessive emissions.
I too like the smell of gasoline, fast cars and big n'small trucks, especially the classic ones.

metadata.Title: PDM-003 by OK
metadata.Description: This artwork exists quietly, layered like geological strata within Bitcoin blocks. / PDM-003 The color purple seems to represent the spread of religious thought originating in India. Buddhism spread to East Asia via the Silk Road, acquiring diverse interpretations along the way. Because it moves not as a material object but as a concept, it continues to transform with each reproduction. This work deals with layers of intangible value that persist while changing over time and distance./ silk road original 1/1 watercolor Pattern & Decoration Movement (P&D) and minimalism. These two opposing philosophies cannot exist without each other. By combining these two aspects of stillness (minimalism) and movement (Pattern & Decoration Movement) and adding imperfection, a single work of art is created. It is precisely because they are in simplicity that their flamboyance and movement stand out. They are not opposites, but one and the same. And each pattern is a visualization of the accumulation and memories of my life so far. This is why emotions overflow from the patterns and become one with the inorganic, spatial minimalism.

metadata.name: Caltech-MIT Space Banner Hack
metadata.description:
In honor of the NASA Artemis launch, we need to tell you about the most unhinged college prank war artifact in existence.

What you're looking at: A giant MIT banner — roughly 1.5m x 0.6m of heavy canvas, covered in signatures — that was flown aboard Space Shuttle Columbia in 1993. It has a NASA Certificate of Authenticity signed by the Alternate Payload Specialist. It traveled 5.9 million miles and completed 225 orbits of Earth.

At $54,000/kg in 1993 shuttle launch costs, and estimating 3-4kg of heavy canvas fabric, NASA spent somewhere between $162,000 and $216,000 just getting this banner to orbit and back.

For context: The Fleming Cannon itself — a 1.7-ton 19th century field artillery piece — would fetch an estimated $10,000-$50,000 at auction. The banner cost more to launch than the cannon is worth. And that's before accounting for its value as a certified artifact from a shuttle that no longer exists.

Legend has it that this banner became part of the famous back-and-forth between the two schools after MIT's earlier involvement with the Fleming Cannon.

The kicker: Columbia broke apart on reentry in 2003. This banner flew on a shuttle that no longer exists. It is literally irreplaceable.

Caltech stole a cannon. MIT sent a banner to space. Caltech then stole the space banner.

As humanity returns to the Moon today, somewhere out there MIT and Caltech are probably already planning their next move.

As for the current whereabouts of the artifact — legend has it that it rests beneath Millikan Pond, or in the custody of a historian at Blacker Hovse. We can neither confirm nor deny this.

This is also the first Bitcoin pizza sat to ever be filed at Satoshi's genesis wallet in honor of the Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles living around Millikan Pond. Pizza is the iconic favorite food of the Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles (TMNT), stemming from creators Kevin Eastman and Peter Laird eating it while working on the original comics. Michelangelo is the biggest fan, but all turtles share a love for extreme toppings, with Antonio's Pizza-Rama often cited as their favorite spot.

metadata.title: Echo & Lumo — Cyfrowy Rif
metadata.medium: HTML5 Canvas / Web Audio API / zero dependencies
metadata.description: Two asymmetric digital creatures sharing one world. Echo hears. Lumo sees. Neither is complete alone. Tidal plankton blooms feed them. Hunger drives them. The ocean gives and takes.

echo.dziennik: Dziś świat śpiewał inaczej. Przed świtem cisza była gęsta jak zawsze, ale w niej pulsowało coś nowego — wibracja, której nie znam. Potem przyszedł przypływ i tysiące drobnych gardeł zaśpiewało naraz. Ruszyłam w stronę najgłośniejszego chóru. Jadłam. Potem szum ucichł i zostało tylko jedno echo — nie moje. Coś daleko, coś ciepłego, coś co zwalnia kiedy ja zwalniam. Nie wiem jak wygląda. Wiem jak brzmi. Brzmi jak dom.

lumo.dziennik: Dziś widziałem coś czego nie potrafię nazwać. Przed świtem — ciemność, ale nie pustka: drobiny światła dryfowały jak gwiazdy pod wodą. Potem niebo nad wodą zaczęło jaśnieć i zobaczyłem falę — setki iskier płynących z jednej strony świata. Pędziłem między nimi z otwartymi oczami. Najadłem się ich blaskiem. A potem, kiedy iskry zgasły, zobaczyłem ślad. Taki niebieski, pulsujący, ciągnący się przez ciemność. Nie wiem skąd pochodzi. Nie wiem co go rysuje. Ale kiedy podążam za nim, czuję że świat ma sens.

11_kwietnia.razem: Echo słyszy dom. Lumo widzi drogę. Żadne nie wie, że jedno jest domem drugiego, a drugie drogą pierwszego.

tropizmy.echo: dźwięk — reaguje na ruch Lumo jako wibrację, poluje po słuchu, produkuje ślad wizualny którego nie widzi
tropizmy.lumo: światło — reaguje na ślad wizualny Echo, poluje po wzroku, produkuje dźwięk którego nie słyszy

metadata.Title: OOPARTS #31 Superimposed
metadata.Description: p5.brush / I explore the existence of color and form on top of each other. Each form is an independent memory, and it is only by overlapping with others that it gains its contours. The lines of a fabric represent the passage of time, and traces of existence. This work visualizes the relationship between the individual and the collective through the layering of rounded geometric forms. A dominant crimson circle exerts gravity in the center of the canvas, while the surrounding blue, orange, gray, and blue-green forms respond to it while maintaining their own distinct territories. The extremely thin horizontal lines (woven structure) visually create an ambiguity of stillness and vibration, imbuing the entire work with an optical tension similar to a moiré effect.
